4.1 Historiography and the History of Philosophy Presentist Approach • A presentist approach to the history of philosophy examines philosophical texts for the arguments they contain and judges whether their conclusions remain relevant for philosophical concerns today. • The main limitation to this approach is that it neglects the various contexts in which past philosophers lived and worked. • In addition to reading philosophical texts too narrowly, the exclusive focus on arguments has been criticized for yielding a profoundly ahistorical understanding of the development of philosophy.

4.1 Historiography and the History of Philosophy Contextualist Approach • The contextualist approach attempts to understand historical philosophy on its own terms, using concepts and ideas that would have been appropriate to the time period in which they were written. • There is a danger that contextualist historians might become interested in the history of philosophy for history’s sake, ignoring the instrumental value of historical philosophy for contemporary philosophers.

4.1 Historiography and the History of Philosophy Hermeneutic Approach • The hermeneutic approach takes the historical context of a text seriously, but it also recognizes that a person’s interpretation of history is conditioned by their contemporary context. • A hermeneutic approach to philosophy can fall prey to a tendency to think about history as culminating in the present.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Egyptian Origins of Classical Philosophy • The understanding that the roots of classical thought lie in Egypt is as old as the ancient Greeks themselves. • In The Histories of Herodotus, the ancient Greek historian Herodotus traces Greek beliefs about the gods, religious practices, and understanding of the natural world to Egypt. • Plato spent 13 years in Heliopolis, and Pythagoras studied mathematics in Heliopolis for over two decades (Boas 1948).

4.2 Classical Philosophy Egyptian and Babylonian Mathematics • Pythagoras almost assuredly learned the “Pythagorean” theorem in Egypt. • A Babylonian clay tablet dating to approximately 1800 BCE, known as Plimpton 322, demonstrates that the Babylonians not only had knowledge of the relationship of the sides and hypotenuses of a right triangle, but also of trigonometric functions (Lamb 2017). • Pythagoras studied with the priests of Heliopolis more than 1,000 years after these documents were created.

4.2 Classical Philosophy The Pre-Socratics • At least a few of the thinkers considered part of this school were contemporaries of Socrates and are mentioned in Plato’s dialogues. o Foremost among these are the Sophists, traveling teachers of rhetoric who serve as foils for Plato’s philosophers. • Researching the pre-Socratics is difficult because so little of their work has survived. • Those who think nature consisted of a single substance are called monists, in contrast to pluralists who see it as consisting of multiple substances.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Prominent Monists • Thales of Miletus and two of his students, Anaximander and Anaximenes, made up the monist Milesian school. • Thales proposed that the basic substance of the universe was water. • Parmenides went so far as to deny the reality of change. o Parmenides was the first person to propose that the light from the moon came from the sun and to explain the moon’s phases.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Prominent Pluralists • Heraclitus held that nothing remains the same and that all is in flux. • Anaxagoras and Empedocles were substance pluralists who believed that the universe consisted of more than one basic kind of “stuff.” • The atomists held the view that the basic substance of the universe was tiny, indivisible atoms. For the atomists, all was either atoms or void.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Pre-Socratic Theology • The pre-Socratic philosopher Pythagoras and his followers comprised a rational yet mystical sect of learned men. • A reminder of their mathematical legacy can be found in the Pythagorean theorem. • Xenophanes rejected the traditional accounts of the Olympian gods. He sought a rational basis of religion and was among the first to claim that the gods are actually projections of the human mind.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Socrates and Plato • As Socrates never wrote anything, he is remembered today because thinkers like Plato featured him in their writings. • The early dialogues feature a skeptical Socrates who refuses to advance any doctrines of his own. Instead, he questions his interlocutors until they despair of finding the truth at all.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Socrates and Plato • Gradually, Plato has Socrates give voice to more positive doctrines. • These include what comes to be known as the theory of the Forms, a metaphysical doctrine that holds that every particular thing that exists participates in an immaterial form or essence that gives this thing its identity.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Aristotle • Aristotle’s works ranged widely across all the main areas of philosophy, including logic, metaphysics, and ethics. • In addition, he investigated natural philosophy, the fields of study that eventually gave rise to science. • At the center of Aristotle’s work was his doctrine of the four causes. He believed that the nature of any single thing could be understood by answering four basic questions: “What’s it made of?” (material cause), “What shape does it have?” (formal cause), “What agent gave it this form?” (efficient cause), and finally, “What is its end goal?” (final cause).

4.2 Classical Philosophy Epicureans • The Epicureans believed that all knowledge was derived from sense experience. • The two principal Greek Epicureans were Epicurus himself and his Roman disciple Lucretius. • Epicurus believed that one should strive to minimize their dependence upon others while limiting the pain in their lives. • Epicurus and Lucretius argued that people must overcome the fear of death if they were going to live happy lives.
4.2 Classical Philosophy Roman Philosophy • Roman philosophical schools were thoroughly grounded in Greek philosophy. • Many Roman philosophers chose to write in Greek rather than Latin.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Rhetoric and Persuasion in Politics • Aristotle wrote a text called Rhetoric in which he sought to analyze rhetoric as the counterpart to philosophy. • Plato generally sought to keep philosophy distinct from politics and was concerned about the messiness of democratic politics in particular. • In Rome, examples of philosophers who were also statesmen include Cicero and Marcus Aurelius.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Stoicism • The Roman Stoics proposed four core virtues: courage, justice, temperance, and wisdom. • The Stoics prized rational self-control above everything else. • The Stoic god is a material entity who exists in nature and meticulously manages it, the material first cause of the universe.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Academic Skepticism • Academic skeptics opposed the Stoic claims that sense impressions could yield true knowledge, holding instead that knowledge is impossible. • Instead of knowledge, academic skeptics articulated the idea of degrees of belief. • The philosopher, orator, and statesman Cicero was the most prominent of the academic skeptics.

4.2 Classical Philosophy Neoplatonism • Plotinus led a revival of Plato’s thought in the late Roman Empire. • Neoplatonism arose during a time of cultural ferment in the Roman Empire, incorporating ideas borrowed from sources such as Judaism and early Christianity. • The key metaphysical problem in Neoplatonism was accounting for how a perfect God could create a universe that was manifestly imperfect.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Defining Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy • Early Jewish and Christian scholars incorporated ideas of classical Greek and Roman philosophy into their theological studies. • As Arab conquerors and traders expanded into the Middle East and Africa, the Muslim world also came into contact with classical philosophy and the natural sciences, adopting and advancing many key ideas.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Early Jewish Philosophy - Philo of Alexandria • Philo of Alexandria published both his philosophical treatises and his personal accounts of his political experiences. • His work represents the first systematic attempt to make use of ideas developed by Plato and other Greek philosophers to explain and justify Jewish scripture. • In reconciling Jewish and Greek doctrines of creation, Philo identifies Plato’s forms as logos, or the thoughts of God.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Early Jewish Ethics and Metaphysics • Following the Roman empire’s destruction of Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah in 70 CE, the Sanhedrin began transcribing the oral traditions so as not to lose them. • These writings would later become the Talmud. Among these writings is the text Ethics of Our Fathers, which provides a moral guide to everyday life. • Later, Jewish scholars also began to explore metaphysics, culminating in the Kabbalah, which examines the relationship between God and the finite world. • The continuation of Philo’s work fell to a subgroup of Jews whose new religion, Christianity, would be adopted by Rome.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Early Christian Philosophy - Augustine • Augustine was one of the most influential philosophers and theologians of late antiquity. • In his Confessions, he used his own life and the story of his initially reluctant turn to Christianity as an allegory for understanding God’s universe and humanity’s place within it. • Augustine famously posits a theory of time that holds that humans experience the temporal present in three different ways: the present anticipates the future and bleeds into the recent past. • Augustine not only articulated Christian doctrine that shaped medieval European philosophy for centuries to come, he raised questions that are still being pondered today.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Boethius • Like Augustine, Boethius was a philosopher who straddled the late Roman and Christian worlds. • Boethius is best known for his work The Consolation of Philosophy. • Extremely popular throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance (Marenbon 2020), his work and influence exemplify how Catholicism incorporated classical philosophy into its worldview. Figure 4.8 In this copy of a 15th-century painting, Lady Philosophy consoles Boethius as he faces death. (credit: “The Figure of Philosophy Appearing to Boethius” by Wellcome Collection/Wikimedia CC BY 4 0)

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Anselm • Anselm served as Bishop of Canterbury and sought to extend the reach of Christianity into the British Isles. • Philosophically, he is best known for a proof for the existence of God, which he elaborated in his written meditation the Proslogion. • Anselm believed that a rational system of thought reflects the rationality inherent in the universe, and that reason and logic can lead people to God.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Islamic Philosophy • In the early years of Islam, theologians prohibited the teaching of Aristotle and other Greek philosophers. This restriction began to give way in the eighth century CE, which led to the flourishing of philosophy in the Islamic world. Figure 4.9 This statue of Ibn Sina in Tehran, Iran, honors this highly influential thinker, who published works in philosophy, medicine, astronomy, alchemy, geography, mathematics, Islamic theology, and poetry. (credit: “Avicenna - Ibn Sina” by Blondinrikard Fröberg/flickr, CC BY 2 0)

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Ibn Sina (Avicenna) • Ibn Sina (called “Avicenna” by Latin writers) was an Islamic philosopher who was influenced by Aristotle. He believed that God created the world necessarily, from all eternity. He also believed that the soul is immortal. • Ibn Sina wrote on logic and the scientific method, talking of various types of proposition and various types of argument. • He pointed out that to make a generalization based on properly tested data, you need to have a cause. • One can discover causes by this type of argument: ▪Fire burns flesh. ▪Fire is hot. ▪Therefore, hot things burn flesh.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Ibn Rushd (Averroes) • Ibn Rushd (called “Averroes” by Latin writers) was another Islamic philosopher influenced by Aristotle. • He argued for the existence of God in at least two ways. He thought that universe was too fine-tuned to human existence to be that way without being designed. This argument is still used today. • He also argued that living things were too complex to have arisen without being designed. Today this view is taken up by advocates of “intelligent design.” • Ibn Rushd believed that God created the world from preexisting matter. • Ibn Rushd believed that souls are immortal, but not individually: he believed that at death we all become part of one soul.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Al-Ghazâlî, the Incoherence of the Philosophers • Al-Ghazâlî was one of the most prominent Sunni Muslim theologians and philosophers. • Writing in a period after the initial establishment of the Sunni sect, he sought to refute various challenges to its teachings from both Shiʽite religious scholars and philosophers.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Late Medieval Philosophy in Christian Europe Bonaventure • St. Bonaventure was one of the Scholastics: Catholic philosophers of the late Middle Ages. • He was influenced by Augustine and somewhat by Aristotle. • He thought “knowledge of divine truth is impressed on every soul,” and God is the source of all knowledge. This is called his “illumination” theory. • He believed that the soul is a thing distinct from the body, with its own kind of matter, and consequently is immortal.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Thomas Aquinas • St. Thomas Aquinas was the most influential of the Scholastics. • He agreed with Aristotle in thinking that the soul is the form of the body but disagreed with Aristotle in thinking that the human soul can separate from the body and so is immortal. • He attempted to prove the existence of God in his “Five Ways”: (1) from motion, (2) from causes, (3) from necessary being, (4) from degrees of being, and (5) from design in nature. • He adopted Aristotle’s virtue ethics to Christian purposes.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Moses Maimonides • Moses ben Maimon, or Maimonides, was a physician, Torah scholar, and astronomer in addition to being a philosopher. • Maimonides proposed that philosophers developed doctrines that do not follow from objective evidence and reason, whereas theologians erroneously interpreted religious texts literally (Bokser 1947). • Maimonides presents a demythologized conception of the divine. Figure 4.10 Although deeply religious, Maimonides opposed both literal interpretations of the Bible and anthropomorphized images of God, arguing that God cannot be imagined or even assigned attributes. This statue of Maimonides stands in his birthplace of Cordoba, Spain. (credit: “Maimónides” by Marco Chiesa/flickr, CC BY 2.0)

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Levi ben Gershom (Gersonides) • Like Maimonides, Gersonides sought to demonstrate the compatibility between Jewish faith and reason. • His most well-known work, Wars of the Lord, takes up the problem of the relationship between Torah, or Jewish scripture, on the one hand and reason on the other.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy The Rise of Reason in the Early Modern Era • In philosophy, the early modern era is delineated by the rapid advancement of natural philosophy, which in turn sparked the scientific revolution. Nicolaus Copernicus • Nicolaus Copernicus, born in Poland and raised by his uncle who was a bishop in the Catholic Church. • At the time, the Catholic Church espoused geocentric model of the solar system, in which the sun and the planets revolve around Earth. Copernicus’s mathematical analysis of the astronomical data indicated that Earth and other planets revolved around the sun.

4.3 Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Philosophy Zera Yacob • Zera Yacob studied Christian, Jewish, and Islamic thought. • Although deeply religious, Yacob argued against the supremacy of one religion over another. Rather, he counseled that people must rely on reason to evaluate religious tracts and traditions—and in this way, reach God. • In Yacob’s view, the stories of miracles arose from false human understanding. Why should engineers study psychology?
COVID PANDEMIC the biggest health emergency of our generation

• Even with the vaccines, an important way to restrict the spread of the virus is restriction of the movement of people. • There are many issues in vaccine delivery – misinformation, availability, distribution, hesitancy. • Therefore, we must depend on behavioral changes and hence, upon human psychology for controlling the spread of infection. Vaccines and Behavior change

• Lockdown: people must stay at home in order to flatten the curve of infection, the effectiveness of the policy depends on whether or not they do. • A fully compliant population could reduce the proportion of those infected. • Thus, many government-led campaigns to encourage people to ‘Stay at Home and Save Lives’. Behavior, then, is clearly critical. • Indeed, controlling the virus also requires getting people to behave appropriately, wear masks — to ‘do the right thing’. Behavior change was critical in the Pandemic

• The trajectory of COVID-19 pandemic was critically dependent on psychological considerations. • Without psychology we could have suffered far greater loss of human life. • Psychology saved lives in covid pandemic. • So many aspects of our individual and collective life, similarly, require understanding of human thinking and behavior. • Psychology can be immensely helpful in your personal and professional journey Why Psychology Matters

What is Psychology? • Psychology - Greek Origin of the word Psyche: "breath, spirit, soul, mind" Logos: Knowledge or study • Was part of philosophy until 19th century. • Earlier definitions of Psychology – science of soul….. Science of mind • Contemporary Definition: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes • Like physics studies matter and biology studies living organisms, psychology studies behaviour and mental processes using scientific methods.

Three important aspects of Psychology 1. Psychology seeks to understand behaviour – Behavior: Overt (i.e., can be directly observed, as with crying) 2. Psychology studies mental processes – mental Processes: Covert (i.e., cannot be directly observed, as with remembering) 3. Psychology is a Science

Defining Science • Science is a body of systematised knowledge. • Science came into existence as a way of answering questions about nature by examining nature directly rather than by depending on religious dogma, past authorities, superstition, or abstract thought processes alone. • Two major components of science – (1) Empirical observation (2) Theory

Observation and Theory • Empirical observation - Information gathered by systematically observing, measuring, or collecting evidence from the real world. • Theory - A coherent set of ideas that explains why and how observations occur and makes predictions that can be tested. • Observation tells us what happens. Theory tells us why it happens.

Example • Empirical observation - Students who receive encouraging feedback from teachers tend to participate more in class. • Theory - Self-efficacy theory in Psychology proposes that believing in one's ability increases motivation and persistence. Positive feedback strengthens this belief. • Analogy: • Empirical observations are like sensor readings from a machine. • Theory is like the engineering model that explains how the machine works and predicts its behavior under different conditions.

Scientific Method in Psychology Observation → Pattern → Theory → Prediction → New Observation • Empirical observations are the bricks; theories are the blueprint. • Psychology advances by continually using evidence to build, test, and improve its explanations.
The Subfields of Psychology: Psychology’s Family Tree

Subfields of Psychology • Understanding sources of change and stability in behavior • Developmental psychology • Changes in behavior over the lifespan (womb to tomb) • Personality psychology • Examines consistencies in people’s behavior over time and traits that differentiate us from one other

Subfields of Psychology • Physical and mental health • Health Psychology • Explores relationship between psychological factors and physical ailments or disease • Clinical Psychology • Investigates diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders • Counseling Psychology • Focuses on educational, social, and career adjustment problems

Subfields of Psychology • Understanding our social networks • Social psychology • Studies how people’s thoughts, feelings and behavior are affected by others • Cross-cultural psychology • Focuses on the similarities and differences in psychological functioning across cultures and ethnic groups

Subfields of Psychology • New frontiers • Engineering psychology • the science of human behavior and capability applied to the design and operation of systems and technology. • Behavioral Genetics • How we might inherit certain behavioral traits and how the environment influences whether we actually display such traits. • Clinical neuropsychology • Focuses on relationships between biological factors and psychological disorders

By the end of this course, you should be able to answer questions like: • Why do we think, feel, and behave the way we do? • How do our minds, our social environments, and our biology shape our behaviour? • What can psychological science tell us about health, learning, decision-making, leadership, use of technology, prejudice, and wellbeing?

Today’s Learning Objectives 1. Describe the precursors to the establishment of the science of psychology. 2. Identify key individuals and events in the history of psychology. 3. Develop a basic understanding of the processes of scientific development and change. 4. Recognize the role of women, and people of color and those from the global south in the history of psychology.

Overview • Introduction and Prehistory • 19th Century Developments: Physiology & Psychophysics • Schools of Thought in Psychology • Role of Women, People of Color and Global South in development of Psychology • Psychology beyond the Western world

Introduction and Prehistory Introduction ▪Short history but long past… ▪Prehistory ▪Ancient Greek philosophers considered mind to be a suitable topic for scholarly contemplation ▪For hundreds of years, various aspects of mental life were studied by philosophers • Psychology as a separate study split from philosophy during mid-19th century

Empiricism • John Locke (1632-1704) and Thomas Reid (1710-1796) emphasized empiricism, or the primacy of the senses in acquiring knowledge. • For example, John Locke believed that children were born into the world with minds like “blank slates” (tabula rasa in Latin) and that their experiences determined what kind of adults they would become. • His views contrasted with those of Plato and the 17th-century French philosopher René Descartes, who argued that some knowledge was inborn in humans
Is perception reality? our senses can, and sometimes do, deceive us. The Ponzo Illusion: the human mind judges an object's size based on its background.

19th Century Developments • Philosophical questions about the nature of mind and knowledge were supplemented in the 19th century by empirical investigations of the sensory systems of the human observer. • Physiology: Research on nervous activity provided an empirical basis for many human functions that were previously considered functions of the mind. • Psychophysics: Attempted to find the quantitative basis for the mind–body relationship by employing an empirical approach. • Evolution: The writings of Charles Darwin in Britain affirmed a theory of evolution based on the empirical evidence of natural selection.

Physiology and Psychophysics ▪The study of nervous activity, sensations, and brain physiology confirmed the benefits of careful systematic empirical strategies. ▪For psychology, these benefits pointed to the possibility of elucidating the physiological basis of mental operations. ▪Hermann von Helmholtz ▪Speed of the neural impulse ▪Senses are fallible but can still be studied ▪Weber and Fechner ▪Measured relationships between experience of senses and external reality (psychophysics)

Advances in Physiology of Brain • Discovery of the neuron, the basic unit of the nervous system – Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal. • Phrenology - interpretation of brain functions - Franz Joseph Gall (1758– 1828) and his student J. G. Spurzheim (1776–1832) • Phrenology attempted to find a physiological localization of mental faculties. • Phrenology held that the degree of a mental faculty or trait possessed by an individual is determined by the size of the brain area controlling that function and that this can be evaluated by measuring the overlying skull area.

Psychophysics • Psychophysics is a type of sensory physiology that emphasized subjective experience in the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and sensations. • Psychophysicts were not strictly psychologists but scholars working their own traditional disciplines –physiology, physics, or natural philosophy. • Studied sensations from several perspectives and emphasized that study of sensations can not be reduced to physiology or physics. • Considered sensations as a reflection of the mind–body problem, rather than as a situation for anatomical and physical study alone.
Schools of Thought in Psychology

Schools of Thought in Psychology – From mid-19th century onwards, psychology came to hold different views about the nature of the mind and the best way to study it. – About the same time, fundamental questions were raised about the definition, nature and scope of psychology giving birth to different schools of thoughts in psychology.

Structuralism Structuralism is a school of thought in Psychology that stresses the basic units of experience and combinations in which they occur. Wilhelm Wundt: • Physiologist and Philosopher. So called ‘Father of psychology’ • Founded the first experimental psychology laboratory in 1879—Leipzig Lab. • Argued that the mind must be studied objectively and scientifically. • Main concern was with techniques used for uncovering natural laws of the human mind—he was in search for the basic unit of thought. Wilhelm Wundt

Structuralism—contd. img6051 • Titchener: Viewed that human conscious experience could be understood by breaking it down into components Approach: • Train subjects in introspection and reporting techniques • INTROSPECTION: looking inside oneself and try to describe what’s going on—understanding oneself. • Trained observers introspected and reported what they experienced • Try to formulate general theories based on their subjects’ reports. Edward Titchener

Functionalism • William James’ (1842-1910) seminal book Principles of Psychology asserted consciousness should be studied as a continuous whole • Combined his studies of physiology and philosophy to create psychology • Proposed Functionalism (what the mind does) as an alternative to structuralism (how mind is structured) William James

The Stream of Consciousness The first and foremost concrete fact which every one will affirm to belong to his inner experience is the fact that consciousness of some sort goes on. 'States of mind' succeed each other in him. If we could say in English 'it thinks,' as we say 'it rains' or 'it blows,' we should be stating the fact most simply and with the minimum of assumption. As we cannot, we must simply say that thought goes on (James, 1892).

Gestalt • School of Psychology that studies how people perceive and experience objects as whole patterns • Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Kohler • “The whole is different from the sum of its parts” • Mental experience depends on patterning and organizing different elements. Example: When we see a tree, we see just that, a tree, not a series of branches.

18 Psychoanalysis • Freud – An Austrian neurologist • Freud is credited with many concepts (e.g., unconscious mind) that influenced 20th century thinkers in psychology and beyond. • In his clinical practice, Freud encountered patients suffering from nervous disorders. Their complaints could not be explained in terms of purely physical causes. Sigmund Freud (1856-1939) Culver Pictures

19 Discovery of the unconscious mind • The mind is like an iceberg. It is mostly hidden, and below the surface lies the unconscious mind. The preconscious stores temporary memories. • Unconscious mind is a reservoir of mostly unacceptable thoughts, wishes, feelings, and memories.

▪Behaviorists like B.F. Skinner (1904-1990) and John Watson (1878- 1958) focused on what was observable and measurable and rejected the idea is that mind could be studied (or worth the effort) ▪The emphasis was on rigorous experimental investigation of overt human and animal behavior. ▪Ultimate goal was finding a relevant S-R relationship and use it for prediction and control of behavior Behaviorism

“Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own special world to bring them up in and I’ll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to be any type of specialist I might select – a doctor, a lawyer, artist…” - Watson 1924 James B. Watson

Cognitive Revolution • Behaviorism’s emphasis on objectivity and focus on external behavior had obscured the study of mind. • By the 1950s, new disciplinary perspectives in linguistics, neuroscience, and computer science were emerging, and these areas revived interest in the mind as a focus of scientific inquiry. This later led to formation of cognitive science. • In the 1960’s, psychologists eschewed behaviorist focus and adopted cognitive approach. • Cognitive approach emphasized that mental processes such as language, memory, and problem solving should play a larger role in understanding human behavior.

Schools of Thought in Psychology at a Glance Structuralism Breaks conscious experience into basic sensations, images, and feelings. Functionalism Explains mental life by the adaptive purposes it serves in everyday living. Gestalt Shows that perception is organized into meaningful wholes rather than isolated parts. Psychoanalytic Emphasizes unconscious conflict, early early relationships, and symbolic meaning. Behaviorism Restricts psychology to observable behavior shaped by learning and environment. Cognitivism Treats the mind as an active processor of information, memory, attention, and problem solving.
Role of Women and People of Color

Women in psychology: Founding mothers • Leta Stetter Hollingworth • Child development and women’s issues • Mary Calkins • First female president of the APA (American Psychological Association) • Karen Horney • Social and cultural aspects of personality
Psychology and Society ▪Psychologists have used science to impact social change ▪In 1936 the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) was formed in the US.

Psychology’s Controvertial Past in US • Historically, Psychologists have taken racist positions and used science to defend racism, eugenic movement (Kamin, 1974). • Supported status-quo: Offered solutions to human predicaments, almost exclusively, in terms of the self-adjustment, leaving the social order conveniently unaffected (Fanon, 1967; Richards, 2003). • Recently American Psychological Association (APA) ‘apologized’ for promoting, perpetuating and failing to challenge racism, racial discrimination, and human hierarchy. 27

Psychology’s contribution to Civil Rights Movement Psychologists and civil rights activists Mamie and Kenneth Clark. • The work of African American psychologists Mamie Phipps Clark and her Husband Kenneth Clark helped to show how segregation negatively impacts the self-esteem of African American children. • This research had impact on the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling that ended school segregation in United States
Psychology in the Global South

Psychology in India • Rich Heritage • More than 100 years of history: The first psychological laboratory in India was established in Calcutta University in 1916. Subsequently Psychology departments were also established in Mysore in 1924, and Patna in 1946 (Sinha, 2017). • Links with Leading Psychologists in the world: Girindra Shekhar Bose, Chairman of the Calcutta University Department of Psychology in 1920s, was closely associated with Sigmund Freud and became a pioneer of psychoanalysis in India. • Many Indians held chairs in world class departments of Psychology around the world – Mahzarin Banaji (Harvard); Anand Pranjpe (Simon Fraser), J P Das (Alberta), etc.

Psychology in the Middle East • Rich Heritage • Ilm al-Nafs - “the science/study of the nafs.” • Depending on the context, nafs may refer to the self, soul, person, or psyche; no single English translation is fully adequate. • Classical scholarship addressed cognition, emotion, bodily health, moral character, habit, suffering, and self- transformation. These discussions appeared across philosophy, medicine, ethics, theology, and Sufi traditions. • Modern scientific psychology began to develop first in Egypt and, to a lesser extent, Lebanon, during the early to mid- twentieth century. • Egypt and Lebanon became important regional centres for psychology teaching, research, and mental-health services.

Psychology in the UAE • Psychology entered many other Arab countries from the 1960s onward. • In the UAE, psychology expanded alongside the country’s rapid development after federation in 1971. • Psychology was established as a separate discipline at UAE University in 1971, initially taught in Arabic within the Faculty of Education before later moving to the social- science context; clinical psychology and postgraduate training developed subsequently. • Psychology in the Middle East and UAE is not simply “Western psychology applied locally.” • It is an evolving field shaped by regional intellectual traditions, colonial and educational histories, and contemporary efforts to build culturally relevant research and practice.

Key Takeaways • Psychology has a long past but a relatively short history as a separate scientific discipline • New ways of studying human experience empirically, especially through physiology, psychophysics, and measurement shaped emergence of psychology as a discipline • Psychology has never been one unified perspective: structuralism, functionalism, Gestalt psychology, psychoanalysis, behaviourism, and cognitivism asked different questions and used different methods • Scientific approaches are valuable, but they are also shaped by historical assumptions about whose experiences count, what is considered “normal,” and which social problems deserve attention. • The discipline has developed globally: India, the Middle East, and the UAE have their own intellectual traditions, institutional histories, and current efforts to make psychology more culturally relevant.

▪ Would people offer to help in this situation?

Kitty Genovese case • Bibb Latané and John Darley (1970) are two social psychologists who taught at universities in New York at the time of Kitty Genovese's prolonged murder, when 38 witnesses failed to call police. • Paradoxically, they thought, it might be that the greater the number of bystanders who observe an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help. • As Latané (1987) put it, “We came up with the insight that perhaps what made the Genovese case so fascinating was itself what made it happen—namely, that not just one or two, but thirty-eight people had watched and done nothing” (p. 78).

The Number of Bystanders: The Bystander Effect Latané and Darley (1970) found that in terms of receiving help, there is no safety in numbers. Dozens of other studies, conducted in the laboratory and in the field, have found what they found: The greater the number of bystanders who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help the victim. This is known as the bystander effect.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BdpdUbW8vbw

Why is it that people are less likely to help when others are present? Latané and Darley (1970) developed a step-by-step description of how people decide whether to intervene in an emergency. Part of this description is an explanation of how the number of bystanders can make a difference.

Interpreting the Event as an Emergency • A key determinant of helping is whether the bystander interprets the event as an emergency—as a situation where help is needed. • If people assume that nothing is wrong when an emergency is taking place, they will not help. • When other bystanders are present, people are more likely to assume that an emergency is something innocuous. Pluralistic Ignorance Bystanders’ assuming that nothing is wrong in an emergency because no one else looks concerned.

Assuming Responsibility Diffusion of Responsibility The phenomenon whereby each bystander’s sense of responsibility to help decreases as the number of witnesses increases. Source of image: Microsoft Office Online.

Features of Good Scientific Theories • Accuracy: Explanations and theories match real-world observations • E.g. Although people say, “opposites attract,” theories that focus on the role of partner similarity do a better job of explaining the observed data

• Consistency: A theory has few exceptions and shows agreement with other theories within and across disciplines. • E.g. The theory of evolution explains many findings across biology and psychology predicting, for example, that humans are better able to solve problems presented in concrete rather than abstract terms Features of Good Scientific Theories

Scope: Extent to which a theory extends beyond currently available data, explaining a wide array of phenomena. E.g. There is a theory that people use mental “short cuts” when making decision rather than weighing every single piece of evidence. This can be seen in consumer purchasing behavior, in romantic relationships, in charitable donations, and in health choices. Features of Good Scientific Theories

• Simplicity: When multiple explanations are equally good at explaining the data, the simplest should be selected. • E.g. The simplest explanation for why “good” people sometimes do “bad” things is because they succumb to some outside influence Features of Good Scientific Theories

Subjectivity and Objectivity in Science The image of a scientist as an objective, unbiased observer to the natural world is not accurate. There are too many choices made by the scientist themselves throughout the scientific process that will impact research results.

Discussion • “fact-value distinction.” Facts are statements about the world and values are our beliefs about the way the world ought to be. • Our values will inform the kinds of questions that we ask and how we ask them, which will in turn influence our results for any single study. • Rather than being cold and dispassionate observers, scientists are active in the process of gathering information about the world and interpreting that information to make sense of it (especially in the social sciences). • As a result, science works best when people with diverse values and backgrounds work collectively to understand complex natural phenomena.

What is the self? • There is no consensus on a conceptual definition • Baumeister (1998) highlights three roots of selfhood – Reflexive Consciousness – Interpersonal Aspect – Executive Function 11

12 Reflexive Consciousness • It is the subjective experience of “conscious attention turning back toward its own source and gradually constructing a concept of oneself” (Baumeister, 1998, p. 680) • The self has unity and temporal continuity

13 Interpersonal & Intergroup Aspect • The self is not only constructed subjectively, but it is affected by the social context as well • Self is “vital for making interpersonal relationships and interactions possible” (Baumeister, 1998, p. 680). • Self is derived from social group membership

14 Executive Function • The self is the agent of all actions and the decision-maker (Baumeister, 1998) • Volution, Agency, Responsibility • It is the essential source of motivation to activate or inhibit actions

Introspection • Introspection: The process by which a person examines his/her mind and mental states. • Privileged Access to our innermost thoughts and desires. • Limitations: – Developmental critique – Children think their parents know them better than they know themselves. – Nisbett and Wilson (1971) showed that people do not really have much privileged access to their selves and do not realise how their minds work. 17

Social Comparison • Leon Festinger (1954) • Social Comparison: people learn about themselves by comparing themselves to others. • Upward social comparison: comparing yourself to people better than you • Downward social comparison: Comparing yourself to people worse off than you. 18

20 Self-Concept vs. Self-Esteem “Self-concept is the totality of the individual’s thoughts and feelings with reference to himself as an object, which eventually explains himself, and the world at large, to himself.”(Rosenberg, 1979, p. ix; Steele, 1988, p. 262) “Self-esteem ... is a positive or negative attitude toward a particular object, namely, the self.”(Rosenberg, 1965, p. 30)

Self-Esteem • People’s self-esteem seems to be responsive to life events. When we reflect on our achievements, self-esteem increases (Sedikides, Wildschut, Arndt, & Routledge, 2008). • Likewise, considering our failures harms self esteem. For example, when people are reminded of the ways they fall short of their ideals, self- esteem decreases (Eisenstadt & Leippe, 1994). • When people with low self-esteem experience negative feedback, their self-esteem suffers further declines (DeHart & Pelham, 2007). • Being ostracized, excluded, or ignored by other people can be psychologically painful and cause reductions in self-esteem (DeWall et al., 2010; Williams, 2001)

Defining Sensation and Perception • Sensation • The detection of physical energy emitted or reflected by physical objects. • It occurs when energy in the external environment or the body stimulates receptors in the sense organs. •Perception •The process by which the brain organizes and interprets sensory information.

Defining Sensation and Perception e.g. Your classmate is poking you. You first sense a poking (sensation), then you immediately know that your classmate is poking you (perception). Recall Psychophysics – the study of relationship between the physical aspects of stimuli and our psychological experience of them.
Sensation • Sense receptors • Specialized cells that convert physical energy in the environment or the body to electrical energy that can be transmitted as nerve impulses to the brain.
Sensation & Perception Processes
Absolute Threshold • The smallest intensity of a stimulus that must be present for stimulus to be detected.

Absolute Sensory Thresholds • Vision: • A single candle flame from 30 miles on a dark, clear night • Hearing: • The tick of a watch from 20 feet in total quiet • Smell: • 1 drop of perfume in a 6-room apartment • Touch: • The wing of a bee on your cheek, dropped from 1 cm • Taste: • 1 tsp. Sugar in 2 gal. water
Difference Threshold • The smallest difference in stimulation that can be reliably detected by an observer when two stimuli are compared; • Also called Just Noticeable Difference (JND).
Weber’s law Weber’s law: A basic law of psychophysics stating that a just noticeable difference is a constant proportion to the intensity of an initial stimulus (rather than a constant amount).

Sensory Adaptation • Adaptation • The reduction or disappearance of sensory responsiveness when stimulation is unchanging or repetitious. e.g. The bath that was almost too hot to enter soon feels too cool; similarly, the cold lake we jump into for a summer swim feels freezing at first, but soon feels only refreshingly cool.

Sensory Adaptation • Advantages and Disadvantages of Sensory Adaptation • Prevents us from having to continuously respond to unimportant information, e.g. traffic noise • Might hamper response to important sensory input such as the smell of smoke. The smell of smoke might not alert you if your house is on fire.

Types of Senses: An Overview • Visual (Vision) • Auditory (Hearing) • Gustatory (Taste) • Olfactory (Smell) • Tactile (Touch) • Vestibular (Balance) • Kinesthetic (Posture & movement) • Organic senses (internal organs & physiological processes)
Vision • What we see (Hue, Brightness, Saturation) • An eye on the eye (Cornea, lens, Iris, Pupil, Retina, Rods & Cones) • How we see colors (Trichromatic theory, Opponent process theory)

Psychological Properties of Light • Light – particles (Issac Newton) or Waves (Thomas Young) • Light = Both particle + Waves = PHOTONS (Albert Einstein) Visible Spectrum The wavelengths that people can see are only a small part of the whole electromagnetic spectrum.
What We See • Hue • Brightness • Saturation

What We See • Hue • Visual experience specified by colour names and related to the wavelength of light. Determined by length of the wave • Brightness • Lightness and luminance; the visual experience related to the amount of light emitted from or reflected by an object. Determined by amplitude (high or low) of the wave. Higher the wave brighter the light. • Saturation • Vividness or purity of colour; the visual experience related to the complexity of light waves. Determined by whether or how much mix of wavelengths is present.

An Eye on the Eye Light enters the eye through the cornea and pupil. The iris controls the size of the pupil. From the pupil, light passes through the lens to the retina, where it is transformed into nerve impulses. The nerve impulses travel to the brain along the optic nerve.

Structure of the eye • Retina • Neural tissue lining the back of the eyeball’s interior, which contains the receptors for vision. • Rods • Visual receptors that respond to dim light. • Cones • Visual receptors involved in colour vision. Most humans have 3 types of cones. • Cornea • Protects eye and bends light toward lens. • Lens • Focuses on objects by changing shape. • Iris • Controls amount of light that gets into eye. • Pupil • Widens or dilates to let in more light.

Crossing of the Optic Nerve Light falling on the left side of each eye’s retina (from the right visual field, shown in yellow) will stimulate a neural message that will travel along the optic nerve to the thalamus, and then on to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe of the left hemisphere. Notice that the message from the temporal half of the left retina goes to the left occipital lobe, while the message from the nasal half of the right retina crosses over to the left hemisphere (the optic chiasm is the point of crossover). The optic nerve tissue from both eyes joins together to form the left optic tract before going on to the thalamus and the left occipital lobe. For the left visual field (shown in blue), the messages from both right sides of the retinas will travel along the right optic tract to the right visual cortex in the same manner.

Why the Visual System is not a Camera • Much visual processing is done in the brain. • Some cortical cells respond to lines in specific orientations (e.g. horizontal). • Other cells in the cortex respond to other shapes (e.g., bulls- eyes, spirals, faces). • Feature-detectors • Cells in the visual cortex that are sensitive to specific features of the environment.
How We See Colours • Trichromatic theory • Opponent process theory
Trichromatic Theory • Young (1802) & von Helmholtz (1852) both proposed that the eye detects 3 primary colours: • red, blue, & green • All other colours can be derived by combining these three.

Opponent-Process Theory • First proposed by German physiologist Ewald Hering in the 19th century • A competing theory of colour vision, which assumes that the visual system treats pairs of colours as opposing or antagonistic. • Opponent-Process cells are inhibited by a colour, and have a burst of activity when it is removed.
Color Vision • Evidence for opponent-process theory: afterimages: images that occur when a visual sensation persists for a brief time even after the original stimulus is removed

Color Afterimage Stare at the white dot in the center of this oddly colored flag for about 30 seconds. Now look at a white piece of paper or a white wall. Notice that the colors are now the normal, expected colors of the American flag. They are also the primary colors that are opposites of the colors in the picture and provide evidence for the opponent-process theory of color vision.

Sensing Sound • Sound • Movement of air molecules brought about by a source of vibration • Eardrum • Vibrates when sound waves hit it • Middle ear - Hammer, anvil, stirrup

Sensing Sound •Inner Ear •Changes sound vibrations into a form in which they can be transmitted to the brain • Cochlea • Filled with fluid and vibrates in response to sound • Basilar membrane • Dividing cochlea into an upper chamber and lower chamber • Covered with hair cells

Auditory Localization • Sounds from different directions are not identical as they arrive at left and right ears • Loudness • Timing • Phase • The brain calculates a sound’s location by using these differences.

Sorting Out Theories of Sound • Place Theory of Hearing • States that different areas of the basilar membrane respond to different frequencies • Frequency Theory of Hearing • Suggests that the entire basilar membrane acts like a microphone, vibrating as a whole in response to a sound

Smell: The Sense of Scents • Airborne chemical molecules enter the nose and circulate through the nasal cavity. • Vapors can also enter through the mouth and pass into nasal cavity. • Receptors on the roof of the nasal cavity detect these molecules.
Sensitivity to Touch: Touch, Pressure, Temperature and Pain

Gate-Control Theory of Pain • Experience of pain depends (in part) on whether the pain impulse gets past neurological “gate” in the spinal cord and thus reaches the brain. • Particular nerve receptors lead to specific areas of the brain related to pain.
Neuromatrix Theory of Pain • Theory that the matrix of neurons in the brain is capable of generating pain (and other sensations) in the absence of signals from sensory nerves.

The Environment Within • Kinesthesis • The sense of body position and movement of body parts; also called kinesthesia. • Equilibrium • The sense of balance. • Semicircular Canals • Sense organs in the inner ear, which contribute to equilibrium by responding to rotation of the head.

Top-Down and Bottom-Up Processing •Top-Down Processing • Perception is guided by higher-level knowledge, experience, expectations, and motivations •Bottom-Up Processing • Consists of the progression of recognizing and processing information from individual components of a stimulus and moving to the perception of the whole
Context Effects • The same physical stimulus can be interpreted differently • We use other cues in the situation to resolve ambiguities • Is this the letter B or the number 13?

The power of context Top-down and bottom-up processing occur simultaneously, and interact with each other, in our perception of the world around us. Bottom-up processing permits us to process the fundamental characteristics of stimuli, whereas top- down processing allows us to bring our experience to bear on perception.

Monocular Cues • motion parallax: the perception of motion of objects in which close objects appear to move more quickly than objects that are farther away. When you are riding in a car for example, the nearby telephone poles rush by much faster than the trees or buildings in the distance.

Takeaways • Sensation and perception are related but distinct processes: sensation refers to the detection and initial encoding of physical stimuli by sensory receptors, whereas perception involves organising and interpreting this sensory information to create meaningful experience • Perception is constructive rather than purely passive. • The brain combines incoming sensory data with prior knowledge, expectations, context, and social-cultural experience. Consequently, people may encounter the same physical environment yet perceive it differently.

From Conditioning to Social-Cognitive Learning What we have covered Classical conditioning: learning through associations between stimuli. Operant conditioning: learning through consequences of behavior. Both approaches explain important forms of adaptive behavior. Where we go next Learners do more than respond automatically to stimuli and rewards. They form mental representations of the environment. They can learn without immediate reinforcement. They can learn by observing models and consequences for others. Learning is not only behavioral; it is also cognitive and social.
Cognitive-Social Approaches to Learning

• Tolman: demonstrated “latent learning” using an operant conditioning paradigm – Rats explored a maze with no reward – Later, under conditions of reward: could demonstrate formation of a “cognitive map” – a mental representation of spatial locations and directions – Indicated that learning had taken place, not “mere” conditioning Tolman’s “latent learning”

E.C. Tolman • Cognitive Theory of Learning – Learning as developing from bits of knowledge and cognitions about the environment and how the organism relates to it. – This was in contrast to the theories of Thorndike who thought of learning as a strict stimulus- response connection.
Cognitive Maps A mental representation of the layout of one’s environment.

Rats and Mazes • Tolman conducted experiments with rats and mazes to examine the role that reinforcement plays in the way that rats learn their way through complex mazes. These experiments eventually led to the theory of latent learning

Latent Learning Latent learning which describes learning that occurs in the absence of an obvious reward Tolman argued that humans engage in this type of learning everyday as we drive or walk the same route daily and learn the locations of various buildings and objects. Only when we need to find a building or object does learning become obvious

• Learning by observing the behavior of another person, or model. • The Model - the person whose behavior the participant watches and imitates • Modeling - The process of observing and imitating a specific behavior Observational Learning – Albert Bandura

Albert Bandura • An influential American psychologist who is known for his work in observational learning, self-efficacy, moral dis-engagement. • Studied the consequences a model has on participants • Bobo Doll experiments • Read - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert _Bandura

Bobo Doll Experiments • Children watched an adult model show aggressive behavior toward a Bobo doll • Three experimental conditions: – The model was praised. – The model was punished. – The model received no consequences for the aggressive behavior.

Vicarious Learning • Learning by seeing the consequence of another’s behavior • Bandura said that reinforcement is not essential for learning to occur, but the expectation of reinforcement affects the performance of what has been learned.

What Have We Learned About Learning? • Classical conditioning: organisms learn that one stimulus predicts another. • Operant conditioning: organisms learn which behaviors bring reward or punishment. • Social-cognitive approaches: organisms learn by forming cognitive maps, observing models, and anticipating outcomes. • Together, these approaches show that learning is associative, behavioral, cognitive, and social.

• Viral protein and DNA were tagged with different radioactive isotopes. Anfinsen’s hypothesis Christian Anfinsen – 1916-1995, Noble prize in chemistry in 1972 • Thermodynamics hypothesis of protein folding • Seminal experiments on refolding of ribonuclease A Anfinsen hypothesized that the primary sequence of a polypeptide dictates shape in aqueous solution – it dictates an array of possibilities and the thermodynamically most favorable result

Anfinsen’s Experiment RNase A – 124 AA long polypeptide • Four disulfide bonds • 8 Cystine residues present • 105 different configurations possible “These results suggest that the native molecule is the most stable configuration, thermodynamically speaking, and that the major force in the correct pairing of sulfhydryl groups in disulfide linkage is the concerted interaction of side-chain functional groups distributed along the primary sequence. “

RNase A – 124 AA long polypeptide • Four disulfide bonds • 8 Cystine residues present • 105 different configurations possible Under appropriate conditions, information needed to reach the native state is encoded in the primary sequence.

What Anfinsen tells us—and what it does not • Supports: primary sequence contains information specifying the native fold. • Supports: the native state is associated with favorable thermodynamics under suitable conditions. • Does not mean every protein folds unaided in a cell. • Does not mean folding is always fast or error-free. • Chaperones can help proteins avoid aggregation and navigate cellular conditions. 12

Protein Folding: Key Takeaways From a linear polypeptide to a functional three-dimensional structure 1 Sequence encodes structure A newly synthesized polypeptide begins as a flexible amino-acid chain and adopts a specific 3D conformation. 2 Folding can be remarkably rapid Many small proteins reach the native state in milliseconds to seconds rather than sampling every possible conformation. 3 Some proteins need assistance Molecular chaperones reduce aggregation and help difficult proteins fold, especially in the crowded cellular environment. 4 Folding is a thermodynamic balance The native state is favored when the overall Gibbs free-energy change is negative: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. 5 The energy landscape is funnel-shaped Many routes can converge on the low-free-energy native structure; kinetic barriers may create intermediates or traps. Many conformations → lower free energy → native state Core idea: folding is biased toward the native state, but the route can include intermediates and chaperone-assisted steps.

Compartmentalization maintains selectivity • Sodium is more concentrated outside the cell, while potassium is in higher concentration inside the cell. • If the charge balance were too skewed, the electrical/ionic forces would overwhelm the structural integrity of the cells and tear them apart. • Therefore all these potassium and sodium ions needs to be balanced by various negatively charged anions. • However, minor and localized imbalances of electrical charge are often seen across the cell membrane, that is essential for cellular processes.

• TRANSPORTER or pump is a protein that contains moving parts and can transfer from one side of the membrane to the other • Transporters can usually move molecules from in to out or out to in; but they do not move simultaneously in both directions • They often move things against their concentration gradients • CHANNEL is a protein with no moving parts • They are usually like pores • They create small hydrophilic holes in the membrane which can only be used by a select few molecules. • Most common are ION CHANNELS as they are specifically for small inorganic ions. • Molecules move across these channels by passive transport Transport proteins Book: Molecular Biology of the Cell, chapter 11

• Some transporters, like the glucose transporter, will move molecules in either direction • After a meal, glucose is higher in the blood than in the cell, so it moves into the cell • After fasting, glucose is higher in the cell than in the blood. So it moves out of the cell • The direction of movement solely depends on gradients. • It’s not that straightforward for charged molecules. • In localized regions of membrane, there are slight differences in charge inside and outside the cell • It means there is a competition between concentration gradient as well as ionic attraction. • Inside the cell is usually negative, pulling in positive ions and repelling those that are negative Concentration gradients and electrical forces drive transport Electrochemical Gradient Book: Molecular Biology of the Cell, chapter 11

• When we deal with charged matter, we are dealing with electricity • When charged things move, current is generated and is a form of kinetic energy • When charged things can’t move, but want to, a charged potential is generated and measured in volts • At the cell membrane, the inside of the cell is negatively charged while outside is positively charged • Opposite attract and these ions want to move • But the membrane does not allow them to move, creating a potential • This potential is known as Membrane Potential and every cell has one • The resting membrane potential of most cells is 20 to 200 mV The membrane Potential

• The forces largely balance • The electric gradient is opposed, but balanced by the different gradients of individual ions • Sodium has an imbalance of force • Any flow of ions across the membrane creates current and changes the membrane potential, making it more positive • Since ion channels are highly selective, and only let specific ion through, to accommodate this change in membrane potential and eventually restore it back to rest, other ion channels must open as well • This implies that opening of ion channels are regulated to change and restore membrane potential • Ion channels are gated and many things can control the gate The membrane Potential

They scrutinized butterfly wings under an electron microscope and discovered the wings’ scales were pockmarked with holes, which are under one millionth of a meter wide, according to The Verge. These holes not only allowed the wings to be lighter, but scattered light so the butterfly can absorb more heat. The holes are random in shape, size, and distribution, according to Radwanul Siddique, lead author of a study recently published online in the journal Science Advances. Computer models helped the scientists realize the shape wasn’t important for absorbing light, but position and order did matter. The scientists utilized hydrogenated amorphous silicon sheets, to create similar structures. A top layer had small holes that could scatter light, allowing it to hit the silicon base. This design collected around twice as much light as others. Standard solar panels only peak at direct noon angles. Few terminologies • Post Translational modification: covalent and enzymatic or spontaneous changes that proteins undergo after synthesis (translation) • Gametes: Reproductive cells • Somatic cells: Body cells like muscle cells or nerve cells • Zygote: Fertilized cell soon after the fusion of gametes • Haploid: Cells containing only one chromosome from each pair • Diploid: Contains the complete set of paired chromosomes • Mitosis: Process of producing Diploid cells • Meiosis: Process of producing Haploid cells

Gamete → Zygote → Embryo GAMETES Before fertilization Specialised reproductive cells Egg + sperm Haploid: one chromosome set (n) ZYGOTE Immediately after fertilization One fertilized cell Formed by fusion of two gametes Diploid: two chromosome sets (2n) EMBRYO After the zygote divides Developing multicellular stage Cells increase through mitosis Begins differentiation and patterning Key distinction: gametes are the cells that unite; the zygote is the first single cell formed; the embryo is the multicellular developing stage.

Cell cycle • The cell cycle is the ordered series of growth and division steps a cell goes through to form two identical daughter cells. • Growth and reproduction of all organisms depend on cell cycle • Cell growth (cytoplasmic increase) is a continuous process. • Prepare itself for duplication – DNA replication, intracellular organelles • It’s subsequent division to identical daughter cells – Cell division

Why does the cell cycle matter? Growth Increase cell number during development and tissue growth. Repair & renewal Replace worn-out or damaged cells in many tissues. Reproduction Cell division supports reproduction in many organisms. One parent cell → two daughter cells

Cell types define cell cycle • Some specialized cells, such as nerve cell or RBCs, don’t divide once formed • Some cells divide on demand – liver cells, WBCs • Most cells routinely divide in order to replenish the dead cells – skin cells, stem cells, gut cells Duration of cell cycle varies according to cell types, but in eukaryotes it is typically 16-24 hours

Checkpoints: pause, inspect, proceed G₁ checkpoint Is the cell large enough? Are nutrients and growth signals available? Is DNA damaged? G₂ checkpoint Has DNA replication finished? Is the DNA sufficiently intact to enter mitosis? Is the DNA replication error or damage free? Spindle checkpoint Are chromosomes correctly aligned and attached to spindle microtubules before separation? Progression can be delayed when a problem is detected.

What is a kinase? An enzyme that can change a protein’s activity ATP + target protein ── kinase ── phosphorylated protein 1. Transfers phosphate Usually transfers a phosphate group from ATP to a target molecule. 2. Changes behaviour Phosphorylation may alter a protein’s activity, shape, location or interactions. 3. Coordinates events Kinases help regulate signalling, growth, DNA replication and cell division. Key idea: phosphorylation can activate or inhibit a protein—it depends on the target.

CDKs: kinases that help time the cell cycle CDK = cyclin-dependent kinase CDK A protein kinase. It phosphorylates target proteins involved in cell- cycle events. Cyclin A regulatory protein. Cyclin levels rise and fall during the cell cycle and help regulate CDK activity. Cyclin–CDK complex The control unit. When appropriately activated, it phosphorylates selected targets to promote cell-cycle transitions. Cyclin accumulates → binds CDK → CDK activity rises → target proteins are phosphorylated

Putting the logic together Progression requires both a “go” signal and the absence of a “stop” signal. Growth signals Cyclin–CDK activation Checkpoint permission Chromosome segregation Two daughter cells If a checkpoint detects a problem, the sequence pauses until the problem is resolved or the cell adopts another fate.

Damage response: pause, repair, or exit Checkpoint pathways convert molecular damage signals into cell-fate decisions. DNA damage / replication stress Checkpoint signaling Repair resume cycle Senescence stable arrest Apoptosis eliminate cell

When control fails: the link to cancer • Checkpoint defects allow damaged genomes to propagate • Chromosome-segregation errors promote genomic instability • Many anticancer strategies target cell-cycle dependencies

Meiosis: two divisions, four cells 1 cell Diploid (2n), DNA already replicated. Meiosis I → 2 cells Haploid (n), chromosomes still doubled. Meiosis II → 4 cells Haploid (n), each genetically unique. Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes pair, cross over and separate. Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate, much as in mitosis.
Prophase I • Longest phase of Meiosis • Spindle Formation • Nuclear envelope starts to break • Homologous chromosomes start to pair • Cross over (Synapse) • Genetic Variation

Variation, and when division goes wrong Crossing over In prophase I, homologous chromosomes swap segments, creating new allele combinations. Independent assortment Each homologous pair lines up independently at metaphase I, giving about 8.4 million chromosome combinations in humans. Random fertilization Any sperm can fuse with any egg, multiplying the possible outcomes further. Nondisjunction Chromosomes fail to separate, giving gametes with extra or missing chromosomes, e.g. trisomy 21 (Down syndrome). Lost checkpoint control Damaged cells keep dividing by mitosis, a hallmark of cancer.

Potency: how many cell types can a cell produce? Totipotent Every cell type, including extraembryonic tissue such as placenta. Example: the zygote. Pluripotent Can generate nearly all body cell types Multipotent Can generate several related cell types. eg: blood stem cells make all blood cells, not neurons. Unipotent A single cell type.

From zygote to specialized cells Zygote one cell Cleavage 2–8 cells Morula compact cell ball Blastocyst inner + outer cells Gastrulation three germ layers Development changes cell fate Cells divide, become organized, and gradually specialize. Key idea More cells does not mean more stem cells: potency and identity change over time.

Zygote and cleavage Rapid mitotic divisions increase cell number before the embryo grows substantially Zygote One cell formed by fertilization 2-cell stage 4-cell stage 8-cell stage Cleavage • Repeated mitotic divisions. • Cells are called blastomeres. • The embryo initially grows little in overall size. DNA replication DNA is copied before mitosis so daughter cells receive genomes. Cell potential Early blastomeres have broad developmental potential, which changes with stage. Approximate duration Cleavage stages occur over the first few days after human fertilization.

Morula to blastocyst Cells begin to organize into distinct populations Morula A compact ball of cells (around day 3; approximate) Blastocyst Outer layer: trophectoderm Contributes to the fetal portion of the placenta and related extraembryonic tissues. Inner cell mass (ICM) Gives rise to the proper embryo; embryonic stem cells derived from it are pluripotent. The important transition Cells are no longer all equivalent: position and signals help establish different developmental fates.

Potency changes during development Zygote Totipotent Can contribute to embryonic and extraembryonic tissues Early blastomeres Broad potential Potential narrows as cell-fate decisions emerge Blastocyst ICM Pluripotent Can form cell types of the three germ layers Tissue stem cells Multipotent Usually form a related family of cell types Specialized cell Differentiated Performs a defined function; usually more restricted Potency = the range of cell types a cell can generate.

STEM CELL Blood Neuron Muscle What makes a cell a stem cell? Self-renewal Divides over long periods without losing its potential to differentiate, and without senescence (biological ageing). Differentiation Gives rise to specialized cell types, such as skin, muscle or nerve cells. An uncommitted, blank precursor that stays unspecialized until it receives a signal. Naturally, it acts as the body's repair system.

How do stem cells divide? Division can preserve the stem-cell pool while also supplying cells that differentiate Symmetric self-renewal Two stem cells Expands the stem-cell pool Obligate Asymmetric division One stem cell + one progenitor Maintains pool while supplying cells Symmetric differentiation Two differentiating daughters Can reduce the stem-cell pool What influences the outcome? Intrinsic cell programs and niche signals: growth factors, neighboring cells, extracellular matrix and mechanical cues.

Differentiation: from flexible to specialized STEM CELL Signals Growth factors, cell contacts influence fate. Gene activity Some genes turn on; others are silenced. SPECIALIZED Specialized cells develop characteristic structures and functions—for example, neurons transmit signals and red blood cells carry oxygen.

Where do stem cells come from? Embryonic (ES) Origin Inner cell mass of the blastocyst Potency Pluripotent Trade-off Most flexible, but ethically contested Adult (somatic) Origin Tissues such as bone marrow, brain, gut and skin Potency Multipotent Trade-off Safer and less contested, but limited Induced pluripotent Origin Adult cells reprogrammed by added genes Potency Pluripotent Trade-off Patient-matched and no embryo, but safety still being tested

Embryonic stem cells: deriving a cell line Fertilization Sperm and egg join Blastocyst Early embryo of 50- 150 cells (about day 5) Remove inner cell mass This destroys the embryo Culture in a dish A cell line self- renews for long periods in vitro Differentiate Change conditions to make skin, muscle or neural cells 50-150 cells in a human blastocyst 220+ cell types in the adult body that ES cells can make ~14 µm human ES cell diameter (mouse: ~8 µm)

Embryonic stem cells: trade-offs Advantages • Flexible: can potentially make any cell type. • Immortal: one line can supply endless cells with defined traits. • Available: embryos come from in vitro fertilization clinics. Disadvantages • Hard to control: difficult to differentiate uniformly into a target tissue. • Immunogenic: cells from a random donor are likely to be rejected. • Tumorigenic: can form tumors. • Ethical cost: destroys a developing human embryo.

Adult stem cells: maintain and repair tissues Tissue stem cells are adapted to particular biological roles Hematopoietic Blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow generate red cells, many immune cells and platelets. Intestinal Stem cells in intestinal crypts continually replace cells lining the gut. Skin / hair follicle Stem-cell populations contribute to epidermal renewal and hair growth. Strength: tissue maintenance. Constraint: many adult stem cells have a narrower developmental range.

Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) Adult cells genetically reprogrammed into an embryonic-like state by forcing expression of key genes. Isolate donor cells e.g., skin cells Add reprogramming genes Culture like ES cells iPSC colonies

iPSCs: promise and open problems Promise • Disease models and drug development: already useful tools. • Patient-matched tissue: nearly identical to the donor, so rejection is probably avoided. • New insight: a way to 'de- differentiate' cells and learn how to repair tissue. Open problems • Viral vectors: in animal studies they sometimes cause cancers. • Delivery: non-viral methods are under investigation. • Equivalence: not yet known whether iPSCs differ from ES cells in clinically significant ways.
